name: Acute Bronchitis

likely: Bordetella pertussis (if prolonged cough >2 weeks, paroxysmal, or known exposure)
pathogens.why: The overwhelming majority of acute bronchitis cases in immunocompetent adults are viral, regardless of sputum purulence (purulent sputum does not reliably predict bacterial etiology). Pertussis should be considered specifically with prolonged paroxysmal cough or known exposure, not treated empirically by default.

investigations.why: Diagnosis is clinical; investigations are reserved for atypical course, prolonged symptoms, or red-flag features suggesting pneumonia.

investigations.test: Chest X-ray (only if pneumonia cannot be excluded clinically)
investigations.why: To rule out consolidation if exam findings are equivocal or symptoms persist beyond expected course.

reason: Clinical findings suggest acute (most likely viral) bronchitis. No fever, no focal chest findings on examination, no hypoxia, and no signs of toxicity. Bacterial probability is low and antibiotics are unlikely to alter the clinical course.

clinicalPearls: Defined as a dry or productive cough lasting <3 weeks, occurring without clinical or radiographic signs of pneumonia; it is most common during winter (p.1537).
Sputum purulence does not distinguish viral from bacterial cause; in acute bronchitis the cough is predominantly viral, whereas bacteria play a larger role in chronic bronchitis (p.1537).
Among acute respiratory infections, only acute otitis media, sinusitis, streptococcal pharyngitis, and pneumonia warrant antibiotics; acute bronchitis is not on that list (p.252).
Acute bronchitis and sinusitis are common at all stages of HIV infection, with more severe disease at lower CD4+ counts (p.1595).
An individual episode of acute bronchitis does not typically cause lasting reductions in pulmonary function (p.1537 context; long-term lung-function data p. respiratory infections section).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute bronchitis is predominantly a viral infection of the lower airways below the vocal cords, caused by common respiratory viruses; the inflammatory airway response produces cough that may be dry or productive, without parenchymal consolidation. Bacterial involvement is uncommon, in contrast to chronic bronchitis where bacteria contribute more prominently (p.1537).
additionalDifferentials: Community-acquired pneumonia (distinguished by a new infiltrate on chest radiography and focal exam findings) (p.1024).
Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis / COPD (p.1024).
Influenza and nonspecific upper respiratory infection, which overlap clinically with lower-tract infection (p.252).
infectionMimics: Pneumonia (cough plus sputum, dyspnea, chest pain, fever, and a new infiltrate point to pneumonia rather than bronchitis) (p.1537, p.1024).
Influenza (overlapping cough and systemic features; can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection) (p.1537).
Pertussis / subacute postinfectious tracheobronchitis (a frequent cause of cough persisting 3-8 weeks) (p.272).
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction presenting as cough and dyspnea, illustrated by a fatal case in which exertional dyspnea and chest heaviness were prematurely labeled acute bronchitis (p.21).
Inhalation of noxious chemicals or smoke, and aspiration, as causes of acute cough (p.272).
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiography should be obtained whenever pneumonia is suspected, to confirm the absence of an infiltrate that defines acute bronchitis (p.1537).

Specific viral diagnosis is generally unnecessary but, when needed, RT-PCR/multiplex respiratory panels are the most sensitive tests; results must be interpreted cautiously because viral genome can persist for weeks after a resolved infection (p.1537).
redFlags: Dyspnea, especially exertional dyspnea or chest heaviness/pain, which should trigger consideration of cardiac or thromboembolic disease rather than acute bronchitis (p.21).
Cough accompanied by sputum, fever, chest pain, or focal chest signs suggesting pneumonia, prompting chest radiography (p.1537).
Hemoptysis or weight loss (raising concern for malignancy or other serious pulmonary disease) (p.272).
Cough persisting beyond a few weeks, warranting reassessment and chest radiography for serious causes (sarcoidosis, lymphoma, lung cancer, tuberculosis) (p.272-273).
harrison.prognosis: Acute bronchitis is a self-limited illness; the cough usually resolves within about 3 weeks, and antibiotics neither speed resolution nor prevent complications in most acute respiratory infections. A dry, irritative postbronchitic cough may linger for more than 2 months, particularly in winter, and a residual subacute cough of 3-8 weeks is common after tracheobronchitis (p.252, p.272-273).
pitfalls: Prescribing antibiotics for acute bronchitis is inappropriate stewardship; roughly half of ambulatory antibiotic prescriptions for acute respiratory infections are unnecessary, and antibiotics cause adverse effects, C. difficile infection, microbiome disruption, and resistance (p.252).
Treating purulent sputum as evidence of bacterial infection is a mistake, since purulence does not reliably indicate bacterial etiology in acute bronchitis (p.1537).

Premature closure: relying on a rapid 'URI/bronchitis' protocol can cause clinicians to miss life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction; a patient who does not look 'sick' may be wrongly assumed to have a benign illness (p.21).
Not eliciting a full dyspnea history (exertional onset, chest heaviness, relief with rest) can lead to a dangerous misdiagnosis of acute bronchitis (p.21).
